name: Bukharan

database_scope.purpose: Sourced reference for Bukharan minhagim and halachic practice. It records what the cited sources say, with a confidence level for each entry, and is not a psak.
database_scope.coverage_note: 29 sourced topics and 7 distinctive customs, compiled from the cited sources in October 2026. Each entry carries a confidence level (well-attested, disputed, regional, needs-review). 20 topics have no community-specific source and are listed under 'gaps' rather than filled with generic text.

identity.primary_origin: Bukhara and the Emirate of Bukhara in Central Asia
secondary_centers: Jerusalem (the Bukharim quarter, founded in 1891) and the rest of Israel
Queens, New York (Forest Hills, Rego Park, Kew Gardens Hills)

languages: Judeo-Tajik (Bukhari): the language of the community's law code, Likutei Dinim (1900)
Judeo-Persian: the older tafsir literature studied in Bukhara, such as a tafsir of Pirkei Avot

subgroups.name: Bukhara (Emirate of Bukhara / historical Central Asia)
subgroups.note: Historic center from the 16th century. Jewish quarters were Mahalla-ye Kohna, Mahalla-ye Now and Amirabad. Rabbi Yosef Maman's reforms began here; he arrived in 1793 and, according to the Jewish Virtual Library, 'served the Bukharan Jews for thirty years, until he died in 1823.' The community was led by a kalantar (chief administrator) and a molla-ye kalan (chief rabbi). The Jewish Virtual Library reports that Bukhara today has 'only 100 to 150 Jews, but probably no more than five families who keep kosher and follow Jewish traditions.'

subgroups.name: Samarkand
subgroups.note: Largest concentration of Central Asian Jews in the 1926 Soviet census (7,740). Chabad influence dates from 1897, when R. Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov settled there and founded a cheder and yeshiva in Samarkand and Tashkent (CrownHeights.info; Chabad.org dates his arrival to 1890). At least one documented Samarkand synagogue prayed in the Bukharian nusach but followed Chabad customs such as reciting all of Tehillim on Shabbat Mevarchim.

subgroups.name: Israeli Bukharian community
subgroups.note: In 1890 seven community members formed the Hovevei Zion Association of the Jewish communities of Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent, which bought land for the Jerusalem Bukharim quarter (Rehovot) in 1891. About 1,500 Bukharan Jews emigrated in the first aliyah, which lasted until World War I (Jewish Virtual Library). According to the Jewish Virtual Library, more than 70,000 Jews have left Uzbekistan since independence, many for Israel and the US. Israeli Sephardic rabbinic authority (Rav Yitzhak Yosef) treats the community as bound by the Shulchan Aruch.

subgroups.name: Queens (New York) Bukharian diaspora
subgroups.note: Centered in Forest Hills, Rego Park, Kew Gardens Hills and Hillcrest. The Jewish Virtual Library estimates about 50,000 of the roughly 70,000 Bukharan Jews in the US live in Queens. The Bukharian Times editor Rafael Nektalov told the Times of Israel: 'We had only one synagogue 30 years ago. Now we have 40.' Institutions include the Bukharian Jewish Community Center, which has Chabad ties. Local rabbis such as Rabbi Nissan Shalomayev publish 'What is the Bukharian Custom?' halachic articles in the Bukharian Jewish Link. Practice ranges widely in observance level.

timeline.event: Jewish sources mention a distinct Central Asian rite, Minhag Khorasan.
timeline.halachic_impact: The pre-Sephardic local rite, later described as the Persian or Khorasani rite.

timeline.event: Bukhara becomes the main center. Links with Iranian Jewry are cut under the Safavids. Religious observance declines, and forced conversion produces the crypto-Jewish chala community.
timeline.halachic_impact: The community could no longer maintain its own religious leadership by the late 18th century.

timeline.event: Rabbi Yosef Maman Maghribi, a native of Tetuan who had settled in Safed, arrives in Bukhara as a fundraising emissary and stays. He serves the community for thirty years, until his death in 1823 (Jewish Virtual Library).
timeline.halachic_impact: Replaced the Khorasani rite with the 'Spanish rite' (nusach Sefarad), set up an academy to ordain rabbis and shochtim, and introduced regular Zohar study.

timeline.event: R. Zecharia Matzliach of Yemen opposes Maman's changes to the nusach.
timeline.halachic_impact: An early, documented dispute over liturgy.

timeline.event: The Hovevei Zion Association of Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent is formed (1890) and buys land for the Jerusalem Bukharim quarter (1891). About 1,500 emigrate before World War I.
timeline.halachic_impact: The Jerusalem Bukharim quarter becomes a center for printing Bukhori religious literature.

timeline.event: R. Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov, sent by the fifth Chabad Rebbe, settles in Uzbekistan and founds a cheder and yeshiva in Samarkand and Tashkent.
timeline.halachic_impact: Beginning of Chabad influence. Bukharian rabbis today trace some customs (sheva brachot outside the home; avoiding kitniyot) to this influence.

timeline.event: R. Avraham Aminov Talmudi publishes Likutei Dinim, in six volumes, in vocalized Judeo-Tajik, with an approbation from Rishon LeZion R. Yaakov Shaul Elyashar.
timeline.halachic_impact: The community's own practical code covering the whole year, distributed free in Bukhara and Samarkand.

timeline.event: Public religious life is suppressed and rabbis are arrested.
timeline.halachic_impact: Home gatherings, above all the yushvo memorial, became the main setting for prayer and teaching. Life-cycle rites were kept more widely than calendar observance.

timeline.event: Mass emigration: according to the Jewish Virtual Library, more than 70,000 Jews have left Uzbekistan since independence, many to Israel and the US, about 50,000 of them settling in Queens.
timeline.halachic_impact: Diaspora rabbis are re-examining which customs are authentically Bukharian and which come from outside influence.

primary_codes: Likutei Dinim (R. Avraham Aminov Talmudi, 1900, Judeo-Tajik; described as the accepted code of law for the Bukharian community)
later_poskim: Ben Ish Chai (R. Yosef Chaim of Baghdad)
R. Ben Tzion Abba Shaul (Ohr LeTzion)
R. Yisrael Chaim Motayev (Mishmeret HaMinhagim; Oseh Chayil responsa)
core_halachic_authorities.decision_principle: Sephardic: the rulings of the Shulchan Aruch are binding (stated by R. Yitzhak Yosef and cited by R. Nissan Shalomayev). A local custom overrides a ruling only if it is old and was set by recognized Torah scholars. Customs traced to later Ashkenazi (Chabad) influence are treated as open to challenge by some Bukharian rabbis.

runtime.practice_baseline: Sephardic practice based on the Shulchan Aruch as read by the Ben Ish Chai, Kaf HaChaim and the Yosef school, supplemented by the community's own Likutei Dinim (1900) and Mishmeret HaMinhagim.

parameters.source: Set by the Sh'elah maintainers for the zmanim page; the community research gives no Bukharian-specific sunset offset.

halacha_index.summary: Bukharian Jews pray in the Sephardic rite. It replaced the older Persian/Khorasani rite after Rabbi Yosef Maman's arrival in 1793.

variants.practice: Persian rite (nusach Paras), also called the Khorasani rite.
variants.source: Encyclopedia of World Cultures, 'Bukharan Jews' (Kotler); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bukhara vii' (Zand)

variants.practice: At least one synagogue prayed in the Bukharian nusach while its leaders followed Chabad customs, such as reciting all of Tehillim before prayers on Shabbat Mevarchim followed by an hour of Chassidut study.
variants.source: Chabad Library (chabadlibrary.org/books/11200004149), memoir describing Samarkand

halacha_index.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'BUKHARA vii. Bukharan Jews', M. Zand, Vol. IV fasc. 5, pp. 530-545
halacha_index.review_notes: Iranica: Maman's reforms included 'replacement of the Khorasani rite with the so-called Spanish rite (nosah sefarad)'. This is corroborated by the Encyclopedia of World Cultures. The Persian rite is sometimes linked to Saadia Gaon's siddur, but only in secondary sources.
halacha_index.summary_he: יהודי בוכרה מתפללים בנוסח ספרד. הוא החליף את הנוסח הפרסי-ח'ורסאני הקדום יותר אחרי בואו של רבי יוסף ממן ב-1793.

halacha_index.summary: One community member reports that Bukharian prayer melodies come from the Central Asian shashmaqam musical system and differ from those of other Jewish communities.
halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, 'How my Bukharian community celebrates Chanukah', Intermountain Jewish News, 19 Dec 2019
halacha_index.review_notes: Single first-person account from Samarkand. Strictly, shashmaqam means 'six maqams' (six modal suites); the article calls it 'six notes'.
halacha_index.summary_he: חבר קהילה אחד מדווח שניגוני התפילה הבוכריים נובעים ממערכת השאשמקום, המסורת המוזיקלית של מרכז אסיה, ושהם שונים מאלה של קהילות יהודיות אחרות.

halacha_index.topic: Birkat Kohanim: father covering his son
halacha_index.summary: During the priestly blessing, a Bukharian father covers his son's head and places his hands on it. Rav Motayev discusses the source of this custom.
common_practices: Father covers son's head and places his hands on it during Birkat Kohanim
halacha_index.source: R. Yisrael Chaim Motayev, Mishmeret HaMinhagim, as reproduced in Hillel Haimov's newsletter (gilyon no. 4)
halacha_index.review_notes: Seen only in a search snippet of the newsletter; the full text was not read. The custom is described as found 'in several communities including' the Bukharian one.
halacha_index.topic_he: ברכת כהנים: האב מכסה את בנו
halacha_index.summary_he: בשעת ברכת כהנים אב בוכרי מכסה את ראש בנו ומניח עליו את ידיו. הרב מוטייב דן במקור המנהג.

halacha_index.summary: Regular Zohar study was one of Maman's reforms and remains central. It is part of the yushvo memorial and of everyday piety.
common_practices: Zohar and Mishnayot at yahrzeit gatherings
halacha_index.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'BUKHARA vii' (Zand); Likutei Dinim as cited by R. Nissan Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 17 Jul 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: Iranica lists 'introduction of regular study of the Zohar' among Maman's reforms. Likutei Dinim describes Zohar study at the yushvo.
halacha_index.summary_he: לימוד זוהר קבוע היה אחד מתיקוניו של ממן והוא נשאר מרכזי. הוא חלק מהישיבו (עצרת הזיכרון) ומהאדיקות היומיומית.

halacha_index.topic: Friday night before washing for bread
halacha_index.summary: A community member asked a halachic Q&A site about two practices: tasting and blessing foods on the table between Kiddush and netilat yadayim, and reciting verses ('LeDavid Hashem ro'i', 'Einei chol') before the blessing over bread. The respondents disputed whether the first practice causes an unnecessary blessing.
common_practices: Eating appetizers with their own blessings before washing (reported)
Not eating bread together with fish (reported)

variants.practice: Calls the blessing before washing questionable, as a possible unnecessary blessing (berakha she-eina tzerikha).
variants.source: din.org.il, 19 Oct. 2015

variants.practice: Defend it as a widespread Sephardic practice.
variants.source: din.org.il, 19 Oct. 2015

halacha_index.source: din.org.il, 'Minhagei Bukhara: mekoram / akhila be-leil Shabbat lifnei netilat yadayim', 19 Oct 2015
halacha_index.review_notes: Reported by a questioner. The site's rabbi called the pre-washing blessing questionable (a possible berakha she-eina tzerikha), while commenters defended it as a widespread Sephardic practice. The page blocked full retrieval, so this is based on the snippet only.

references.title: מנהגי בוכרה - מקורם / אכילה בליל שבת לפני נטילת ידים

halacha_index.topic_he: ליל שבת לפני נטילת ידיים לסעודה
halacha_index.summary_he: חבר קהילה שאל אתר שו"ת הלכתי על שני מנהגים: טעימת מאכלים וברכה עליהם על השולחן בין הקידוש לנטילת ידיים, ואמירת פסוקים ("לדוד ה' רועי", "עיני כל") לפני ברכת הלחם. המשיבים נחלקו אם המנהג הראשון גורם לברכה שאינה צריכה.

halacha_index.summary: The traditional Bukharian sukkah is hung with colorful silk and woven fabrics, and the floor is covered with embroidered rugs and cushions instead of chairs. This reportedly continues in New York and Israel.
halacha_index.source: Jewish Journal, 'Around the Jewish World, Distinct Traditions for Sukkot', 12 Oct 2011, citing Esther Shkalim, A Mosaic of Israel's Traditions
halacha_index.review_notes: Second-hand, and only the search snippet was read. This is decorative custom, not halacha.
halacha_index.summary_he: הסוכה הבוכרית המסורתית מקושטת בבדי משי ובאריגים צבעוניים, והרצפה מכוסה בשטיחים רקומים ובכריות במקום כסאות. לפי הדיווחים המנהג נמשך בניו יורק ובישראל.

halacha_index.summary: In Samarkand families lit a flat oil menorah with cotton wicks, preparing olive oil especially for the holiday because local oil was cottonseed. Children received gifts on only one night. Fried dough cookies (hushquiliq) are a holiday food.
common_practices: Flat oil menorah with cotton wicks

variants.practice: A standing menorah is now common for safety, though the author still prefers oil to candles.
variants.source: Khaimov, Intermountain Jewish News, 2019

halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, 'How my Bukharian community celebrates Chanukah', Intermountain Jewish News, 19 Dec 2019
halacha_index.review_notes: Single first-person account (Samarkand). The cookie recipe is credited to Amnun Kimyagarov, Classic Central Asian (Bukharian) Jewish Cuisine and Customs (2010).

references.title: How my Bukharian community celebrates Chanukah

halacha_index.summary_he: בסמרקנד הדליקו המשפחות חנוכייה שטוחה של שמן עם פתילות כותנה, והכינו שמן זית במיוחד לחג כי השמן המקומי היה שמן גרעיני כותנה. הילדים קיבלו מתנות רק בלילה אחד. עוגיות בצק מטוגנות (חושקיליק) הן מאכל החג.

halacha_index.summary: There is no single Bukharian practice. A Bukharian rabbi documents three customs, and a community writer reports that the community eats kitniyot.
common_practices: Rice eaten; rice dishes are central to the cuisine

variants.subgroup: A small part of the community
variants.practice: No rice and no other legumes.
variants.source: Bechori Yisrael vol. 4, 5:1, cited by R. N. Shalomayev

variants.practice: Rice eaten but other legumes avoided, because rice is a staple and forbidding it would be a decree the public could not bear.
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 10 Apr 2024

variants.practice: No rice on the first two days of Pesach; rice eaten on the remaining days. Dr. Giora Fuzailov attributes this to respect for Ashkenazi emissaries; another explanation points to Ashkenazi refugees hosted during WWII.
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev citing Fuzailov and the Haggadah of the Bukharian Jews by R. Bechor Baruch (Malayev)

variants.practice: 'We eat kitniyot, so we always have a variety of rice dishes.'
variants.source: Manashe Khaimov, My Jewish Learning, 6 Apr 2020

halacha_index.source: R. Nissan Shalomayev, 'Bukharian Custom of Kitniyot on Pesach', Bukharian Jewish Link, 10 Apr 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: Shalomayev states that avoiding kitniyot 'is not an old custom': Likutei Dinim (Siman 145:4) only suggests following the Rama as a 'good' custom and does not record it as the Bukharian practice. He suggests Chabad influence. Whether the custom can be annulled (hatarat nedarim) is referred to a halachic authority.

references.title: Bukharian Custom of Kitniyot on Pesach

halacha_index.summary_he: אין מנהג בוכרי אחד. רב בוכרי מתעד שלושה מנהגים, וכותב מהקהילה מדווח שהקהילה אוכלת קטניות.

halacha_index.summary: Bukharian custom is to check rice for wheat kernels three times before Pesach use, away from children and distractions.
halacha_index.source: R. Rafael Shamsiyev, Bechori Yisrael vol. 4, 5:1, cited in R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 10 Apr 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: Shalomayev adds that someone pressed for time may rely on one very thorough check, since rice is cleaner today. That is his own note, not part of the custom.

references.title: Bukharian Custom of Kitniyot on Pesach

halacha_index.summary_he: המנהג הבוכרי הוא לבדוק את האורז שלוש פעמים לפני השימוש בו בפסח, הרחק מילדים ומהסחות דעת, כדי לוודא שאין בו גרעיני חיטה.

halacha_index.summary: Some families still bake their own matzah in the old-country style, resembling laffa flatbread. Many in the US now use store-bought matzah. Matzah is eaten dipped in a meat soup (oshi masozgoshak).
halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, 'Bukharian Passover Traditions and Recipes', My Jewish Learning, 6 Apr 2020
halacha_index.review_notes: Single community-writer source. No halachic source on Bukharian matzah baking was found.
halacha_index.summary_he: משפחות אחדות עדיין אופות מצה בעצמן בסגנון הארץ הישנה, הדומה ללאפה. רבים בארצות הברית משתמשים היום במצה מוכנה מהחנות. אוכלים את המצה כשהיא טבולה במרק בשר (אושי מסוזגושאק).

halacha_index.summary: Participants sit by seniority, elders nearest the host, traditionally men and women on opposite sides. Young people bring water around for hand-washing. Cups are rinsed with water after each cup so wines are not mixed. The seder plate has a lamb foot instead of a shank and romaine lettuce instead of horseradish. The charoset is chaliko (raisins, walnuts and apple, sometimes dried apricot).
common_practices: Cup rinsed between cups (an honored role)

variants.practice: Some families now alternate seating man-woman-woman-man.
variants.source: Khaimov, My Jewish Learning, 2020

halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, 'Bukharian Passover Traditions and Recipes', My Jewish Learning, 6 Apr 2020
halacha_index.review_notes: Detailed, but from a single community source.
halacha_index.summary_he: המסובים יושבים לפי ותק, הזקנים הקרובים ביותר לבעל הבית, ובדרך כלל גברים ונשים בצדדים מנוגדים. צעירים מביאים מים לנטילת ידיים. שוטפים את הכוסות במים אחרי כל כוס כדי שהיינות לא יתערבבו. בקערת הסדר יש רגל כבש במקום זרוע, וחסה רומית במקום חזרת. החרוסת היא חליקו (צימוקים, אגוזי מלך ותפוח, לפעמים משמש מיובש).

halacha_index.summary: Bukharians have their own Haggadah containing Bukhori (Judeo-Tajik) songs in Hebrew letters. They do not sing Echad Mi Yodea; they sing 'Yakumin Ki Medonad' in Bukhori, and have their own version of Chad Gadya called 'Jon Buzghole'.
common_practices: Yakumin Ki Medonad in place of Echad Mi Yodea
halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, My Jewish Learning, 6 Apr 2020
halacha_index.review_notes: A Haggadah of the Bukharian Jews by R. Bechor Baruch (Malayev) is cited by R. Shalomayev but was not opened. Shimon Hakham's 1904 Bukhori Haggadah translation is known only from a secondary lead.

references.title: Bukharian Custom of Kitniyot on Pesach

halacha_index.summary_he: לבוכרים יש הגדה משלהם ובה שירים בבוכורי (יהודית-טג'יקית) באותיות עבריות. הם אינם שרים "אחד מי יודע"; הם שרים "יקומין כי מדונד" בבוכורי, ויש להם גרסה משלהם ל"חד גדיא" בשם "ז'ון בוזגולה".

halacha_index.summary: Before the afikoman is found, an elder goes around the table asking who has it and lightly 'whips' everyone with a towel, so they feel a little of the slaves' pain. Seders include skits of escaping Egypt.
halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, My Jewish Learning, 6 Apr 2020
halacha_index.review_notes: Single source.
halacha_index.summary_he: לפני שמוצאים את האפיקומן, זקן מסובב סביב השולחן ושואל מי נטל אותו, ו"מצליף" קלות בכולם במגבת, כדי שירגישו מעט מכאבם של העבדים. בסדרים יש מערכונים על יציאת מצרים.

halacha_index.summary: Men and women wear the jomah, a colorful kaftan embroidered with gold, at the seder as a sign of royalty and freedom.
common_practices: Jomah kaftan worn at the seder

variants.practice: Families wear Bukharian clothing on seder night.
variants.source: Adina Meshulam, 'Al ha-kippa ha-bukharit u-she'ar minhagim', HaKesher HaRav Dori, 2016

halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, My Jewish Learning, 6 Apr 2020
halacha_index.review_notes: Two independent community accounts, one from the US and one from Israel. The Israeli account was seen only in a search snippet.
halacha_index.summary_he: גברים ונשים לובשים בליל הסדר את הג'ומה, קפטן צבעוני רקום בזהב, כסימן למלכות ולחירות.

halacha_index.topic: The Nine Days and Tisha B'Av
halacha_index.summary: Bukharan communities reportedly read different kinot in the synagogue on each day from Rosh Chodesh Av to Tisha B'Av. Shochtim hid their slaughtering knives and walked fully barefoot on the night of Tisha B'Av.
common_practices: Daily kinot from Rosh Chodesh Av
Shochtim put away knives; barefoot on the night of the 9th
halacha_index.source: Ortal Mogus, 'Kotzim al ha-mitpallelim...: minhagei Tisha B'Av misaviv la-olam', Ynet, 30 Jul 2020 (drawing on the 'HaLuach HaIvri' project)
halacha_index.review_notes: Journalistic compilation. The Bukhara passage was seen in the search snippet; the fetched text cut off before it. Needs confirmation from a Bukharian kinot book or minhag work.
halacha_index.summary_he: לפי הדיווחים, בקהילות בוכרה קראו בבית הכנסת קינות שונות בכל יום מראש חודש אב עד תשעה באב. השוחטים הסתירו את סכיני השחיטה והלכו יחפים לחלוטין בליל תשעה באב.

halacha_index.summary: According to a cited bibliographic source, a Judeo-Persian translation and commentary (tafsir) of Pirkei Avot was studied in Bukhara and its districts on the Shabbatot of the summer cycle beginning after Pesach.
common_practices: Summer Shabbat study of Avot in Judeo-Persian translation
halacha_index.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'JUDEO-PERSIAN COMMUNITIES ix. Judeo-Persian Literature', citing Ya'ari (1942)
halacha_index.review_notes: Seen in the search snippet only. The snippet's end date ('Shmini Atzeret [the last day of Rosh-Hashanah]') looks garbled and should be checked against the original.
halacha_index.summary_he: לפי מקור ביבליוגרפי מצוטט, תרגום ופירוש (תפסיר) יהודי-פרסי של פרקי אבות נלמד בבוכרה ובסביבתה בשבתות מחזור הקיץ, שמתחיל אחרי פסח.

halacha_index.topic: Separate ovens for bread and meat pastry
halacha_index.summary: In Samarkand, bread baked in an oven used for meat may not be eaten with dairy, so bread was baked in one tandir and meat samsa in another.
common_practices: Dedicated tandir ovens for bread vs. meat pastries
halacha_index.source: Manashe Khaimov, 'How My Bukharian Jewish Community Celebrates Hanukkah', SAMi blog
halacha_index.review_notes: Seen in the search snippet only. This matches general halacha on bread baked with meat (Shulchan Aruch YD 97), but is reported as local practice.
halacha_index.summary_he: בסמרקנד אסור לאכול עם חלב לחם שנאפה בתנור ששימש לבשר, ולכן אפו לחם בתנדיר אחד וסמסה בשר באחר.

halacha_index.summary: Maman's academy ordained shochtim. Historically, Bukharian khakhams combined the roles of rabbi, shochet, mohel and cantor.
halacha_index.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'BUKHARA vii' (Zand); Encyclopedia of World Cultures, 'Bukharan Jews' (Kotler)
halacha_index.review_notes: Historical and institutional. No current Bukharian-specific shechita stringency was found.
halacha_index.summary_he: הישיבה של ממן הסמיכה שוחטים. מבחינה היסטורית חכמים בוכרים כיהנו כרב, שוחט, מוהל וחזן גם יחד.

halacha_index.summary: The poskim the community follows disagree. The Ben Ish Chai and Kaf HaChaim (168:137) follow the Taz: a filled pastry is mezonot unless a meal's worth is eaten. R. Ovadia Yosef follows the Magen Avraham: meat-filled dough is hamotzi.

variants.subgroup: Followers of Ben Ish Chai / Kaf HaChaim
variants.practice: Mezonot (unless a meal-sized amount is eaten).
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 8 May 2024

variants.practice: Hamotzi.
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 8 May 2024

halacha_index.source: R. Nissan Shalomayev, 'Blessing on Samsa/Gozhgidzha or Beechak', Bukharian Jewish Link, 8 May 2024 (Shulchan Aruch OC 168; Taz 168:6; Magen Avraham 168:44)
halacha_index.review_notes: The article has a section 'Minhag of the Bucharian Jews' citing Likutei Dinim, but the fetched text cut off before it. The Bukharian ruling itself has not been captured. Send to rabbinic review.
halacha_index.topic_he: ברכה על סמסה / גוז'גי'ז'ה (בצק ממולא בשר)
halacha_index.summary_he: הפוסקים שהקהילה הולכת אחריהם חלוקים. הבן איש חי וכף החיים (קסח:קלז) הולכים אחרי הט"ז: מאפה ממולא הוא מזונות, אלא אם אוכלים שיעור סעודה. רבי עובדיה יוסף הולך אחרי המגן אברהם: בצק ממולא בשר הוא המוציא.

halacha_index.summary: Circumcision (milo) is on the eighth day. Historically khakhams served as mohalim. Bukharian Jews of earlier generations kept chillah, a confinement after birth and after marriage during which women did not leave the house.
halacha_index.source: Encyclopedia of World Cultures, 'Bukharan Jews' (Kotler); R. N. Shalomayev, 'Sheva Brachot In Restaurants And Shuls', Bukharian Jewish Link, 28 Feb 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: Shalomayev calls chillah a 'superstitious custom' and gives no length; a commonly repeated '40 days' is not documented in the sources read. No source was found for brit-eve vigils, choice of sandak, or pidyon haben.

references.title: Sheva Brachot In Restaurants And Shuls

halacha_index.summary_he: המילה (מילו) נעשית ביום השמיני. מבחינה היסטורית חכמים שימשו מוהלים. יהודי בוכרה בדורות קודמים שמרו על "חילה", תקופת התבודדות אחרי לידה ואחרי נישואין שבה נשים לא יצאו מהבית.

halacha_index.summary: At 13 a boy goes through a coming-of-age ceremony called tefillinbandon, literally 'tefillin-binding'.
halacha_index.source: Encyclopedia of World Cultures, 'Bukharan Jews' (I. Kotler), via Encyclopedia.com
halacha_index.review_notes: The name is attested, but the ceremony itself is not described in any source read. No bat mitzvah custom was found.
halacha_index.summary_he: בגיל 13 עובר הנער טקס בגרות בשם תפילינבנדון, כלומר "קשירת תפילין" מילולית.

halacha_index.summary: The traditional wedding week includes a bride price (kalin) and a dowry, the bride's visit to the bath or mikveh, a women's henna celebration or eyebrow rite, writing of the ketubah, and the chuppah (hupo) followed by the feast (tuy). Sources disagree on which day each step falls.

variants.practice: Sunday: bride taken to the baths. Monday: women celebrate painting the bride's hands with henna. Wednesday: chuppah by a rabbi, then the feast.
variants.source: Encyclopedia of World Cultures, 'Bukharan Jews' (Kotler)

variants.practice: Sunday: mikveh. Monday: kosh-chinon (first shaping of the bride's eyebrows). Tuesday: ketubah written.
variants.source: HaMichlol, 'Nisuim be-yahadut Bukhara' (citing Dan Benaya Seri, Chatuna Bukharit, Keter 2006)

halacha_index.source: Encyclopedia of World Cultures, 'Bukharan Jews' (I. Kotler)
halacha_index.review_notes: The two sources disagree on Monday's rite (henna vs. eyebrows). Treat this as historical ethnography, not current halacha. Levirate marriage and chalitza ('halitso') were practiced historically.
halacha_index.summary_he: שבוע החתונה המסורתי כולל מוהר (קלין) ונדוניה, ביקור הכלה במרחץ או במקווה, חגיגת חינה של נשים או טקס העיצוב של הגבות, כתיבת הכתובה והחופה (הופו) ואחריה המשתה (טוי). המקורות חלוקים באיזה יום חל כל שלב.

halacha_index.summary: Before the wedding, and before her mikveh immersion according to one account, married women gather while a koshchin shapes the bride's eyebrows for the first time with a blade and thread, with special songs and food.
common_practices: First eyebrow shaping of the bride

variants.practice: Still performed by some brides, before the mikveh.
variants.source: Deborah Danan, 'The Bukhari Renaissance Woman', Jewish Journal

variants.practice: Monday, after the Sunday mikveh.
variants.source: HaMichlol, 'Nisuim be-yahadut Bukhara'

halacha_index.source: Deborah Danan, 'The Bukhari Renaissance Woman', Jewish Journal
halacha_index.review_notes: The custom itself is attested by two sources, but they disagree on whether it comes before or after the mikveh. Both were seen as search snippets.
halacha_index.summary_he: לפני החתונה, ולפי גרסה אחת לפני טבילתה במקווה, מתכנסות נשים נשואות בשעה שקושצ'ין מעצבת את גבות הכלה בפעם הראשונה בעזרת סכין וחוט, בשירים מיוחדים ובמאכלים.

halacha_index.topic: Sheva brachot outside the couple's home
halacha_index.summary: Many Bukharians today recite all seven blessings at sheva brachot meals held in restaurants or other homes. A Queens Bukharian rabbi argues the original custom was to recite them only in the couple's home, following the Shulchan Aruch (EH 62) and Likutei Dinim.
common_practices: Current widespread practice: full sheva brachot at any venue

variants.practice: Sheva brachot only in the couple's (usually the parents') home, where the couple stayed during chillah.
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev citing Likutei Dinim 131:1 and Mishmeret HaMinhagim 11

variants.practice: All seven blessings recited outside the home; Shalomayev attributes this to Chabad emissaries in Uzbekistan.
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 28 Feb 2024

halacha_index.source: R. Nissan Shalomayev, 'Sheva Brachot In Restaurants And Shuls', Bukharian Jewish Link, 28 Feb 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Motayev reports that the elders said there was 'no custom' of reciting the blessings outside the home. Shalomayev acknowledges that 'some current Bukharian rabbis' accept the current practice. Yalkut Yosef (Sova Semachot 17:6) requires the couple's home, a minyan and two panim chadashot. The first night may be held anywhere.

references.title: Sheva Brachot In Restaurants And Shuls

halacha_index.topic_he: שבע ברכות מחוץ לבית בני הזוג
halacha_index.summary_he: בוכרים רבים אומרים היום את כל שבע הברכות בסעודות שבע ברכות הנערכות במסעדות או בבתים אחרים. רב בוכרי מקווינס טוען שהמנהג המקורי היה לאומרן רק בבית בני הזוג, על פי השולחן ערוך (אבן העזר סב) ו"לקוטי דינים".

halacha_index.summary: On a parent's yahrzeit, families host a gathering where Torah scholars study Mishnayot and Zohar and recite Kaddish and hashkava, followed by a meal. Likutei Dinim calls it 'leil yeshiva' (yushvo).
common_practices: Customs begin from the Shabbat before the yahrzeit

variants.practice: Held by wealthy families; praised only if the study is serious and the meal has words of Torah. If it becomes frivolous, the money should go to the poor instead.
variants.source: Likutei Dinim, trans. R. Hillel Haimoff, cited by R. N. Shalomayev

variants.practice: The yushvo became the main covert setting for prayer and religious teaching.
variants.source: Prof. Alanna Cooper, cited by R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 31 Jul 2024

variants.practice: Often held as a large restaurant or catering-hall dinner with speeches and poetry. A local rabbi criticizes missing blessings and heavy drinking and urges a return to an evening of Torah study.
variants.source: R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 31 Jul 2024

halacha_index.source: R. Nissan Shalomayev, 'All You Need To Know About Yushvo', Bukharian Jewish Link, 17 Jul 2024 (excerpt from Hillel Omer)
halacha_index.review_notes: Corroborated by Alanna Cooper (academic) and by Encyclopaedia Iranica on how widely life-cycle observance continued. Shulchan Aruch YD 376:4 and 402:12 record fasting on a parent's yahrzeit; the yushvo is presented as a later substitute based on Torah study and charity.
halacha_index.summary_he: ביום היארצייט של הורה המשפחות מארחות התכנסות שבה תלמידי חכמים לומדים משניות וזוהר ואומרים קדיש והשכבה, ואחריה סעודה. "לקוטי דינים" קורא לה "ליל ישיבה" (ישיבו).

halacha_index.topic: Monthly yushvo in the first year
halacha_index.summary: During the first year of mourning, a yushvo is held each month on the date of death, in addition to the shiva practices common to all Jews.
common_practices: Monthly memorial meal on the date of death during year one
halacha_index.source: Alanna Cooper, 'Who Are the Bukharan Jews?', My Jewish Learning
halacha_index.review_notes: Academic author. The passage was seen in the search snippet; the fetched text cut off earlier.
halacha_index.summary_he: במשך שנת האבל הראשונה נערך ישיבו בכל חודש בתאריך הפטירה, נוסף על דיני השבעה הנוהגים אצל כל היהודים.

halacha_index.topic: Kaddish and women's roles in mourning
halacha_index.summary: Sons recite Kaddish daily for the first year and annually afterwards. Historically each neighborhood's women elected a kayvani, who organized the women's side of weddings, instructed brides, and organized the mourners' performance.
common_practices: Sons' daily Kaddish in year one
halacha_index.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'BUKHARA vii' (Zand); Encyclopedia of World Cultures (Kotler)
halacha_index.review_notes: The kayvani office was historical Bukhara. Seen in the search snippet of the Iranica article.

references.title: Religion and expressive culture - Bukharan Jews

halacha_index.summary_he: בנים אומרים קדיש מדי יום בשנה הראשונה ובכל שנה אחריה. מבחינה היסטורית נשות כל שכונה בחרו "קיוואני", שארגנה את צד הנשים בחתונות, הדריכה כלות וארגנה את מילוי תפקידי האבלים.

halacha_index.summary: Today the custom is to recite hashkava (the memorial prayer) even between aliyot, not only once at the end of the reading as the Rama records. It is linked to a charity pledge, and it is preferable that the children of the deceased recite it.
halacha_index.source: R. Nissan Shalomayev, 'History Of Hashkavah Prayer For The Deceased', Bukharian Jewish Link, 27 Mar 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: Seen in the search snippet. It is not explicit whether this describes Bukharian practice specifically or Sephardic practice generally.

references.title: History Of Hashkavah Prayer For The Deceased

halacha_index.summary_he: כיום נוהגים לומר השכבה (תפילת הזיכרון) גם בין העליות, ולא רק פעם אחת בסוף הקריאה כפי שהרמ"א מביא. היא קשורה בנדר צדקה, ורצוי שילדי הנפטר יאמרו אותה.

halacha_index.summary: Practical halacha reached the community through vocalized Judeo-Tajik works such as Likutei Dinim (6 vols., 1900), written for 'all strata of the people including women and children'. Religious texts were also widely translated into Bukhori, including a Haggadah and Megillat Esther.
common_practices: Likutei Dinim as the accepted code
Bukhori translations of liturgy and Tanakh
halacha_index.source: Bucharim.com, 'Echad haya Avraham' (biography of R. Avraham Aminov Talmudi); R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 28 Feb 2024
halacha_index.review_notes: Likutei Dinim received an approbation from Rishon LeZion R. Yaakov Shaul Elyashar and was distributed free in Bukhara and Samarkand.
halacha_index.summary_he: ההלכה המעשית הגיעה לקהילה דרך חיבורים מנוקדים ביהודית-טג'יקית כמו "לקוטי דינים" (6 כרכים, 1900), שנכתב ל"כל שכבות העם, כולל נשים וילדים". גם טקסטים דתיים תורגמו בהרחבה לבוכורי, ובהם הגדה ומגילת אסתר.

unique_minhagim.name: Yushvo
unique_minhagim.description: Yahrzeit or memorial gathering with Mishnayot and Zohar study, Kaddish, hashkava and a meal. Held monthly in the first year and annually after that.
unique_minhagim.when: Yahrzeit; monthly during the first year of mourning
unique_minhagim.source: Likutei Dinim via R. N. Shalomayev, Bukharian Jewish Link, 17 Jul 2024; Alanna Cooper, My Jewish Learning
unique_minhagim.description_he: יארצייט או התכנסות זיכרון עם לימוד משניות וזוהר, קדיש, השכבה וסעודה. נערכת מדי חודש בשנה הראשונה ומדי שנה אחר כך.

unique_minhagim.name: Kushelik at the yushvo
unique_minhagim.description: Paper-thin fried dough dusted with sugar, eaten before the rest of the yushvo meal and described as symbolizing the soul's ascent.
unique_minhagim.source: My Jewish Learning (The Nosher), 'Bukharian Jews Honor Lost Loved Ones With This Traditional Dinner'
unique_minhagim.description_he: בצק מטוגן דק כנייר ומפוזר בסוכר, שאוכלים לפני שאר סעודת הישיבו, ומתוארת כסמל לעליית הנשמה.

unique_minhagim.name: Jomah at the seder
unique_minhagim.description: Gold-embroidered kaftan worn by men and women at the seder.
unique_minhagim.description_he: קפטן רקום בזהב שגברים ונשים לובשים בליל הסדר.

unique_minhagim.name: Yakumin Ki Medonad and Jon Buzghole
unique_minhagim.description: Bukhori-language seder songs, sung instead of Echad Mi Yodea and as a Bukharian Chad Gadya.
unique_minhagim.description_he: שירי סדר בשפת הבוכורי, הנשרים במקום "אחד מי יודע" וכגרסה בוכרית של "חד גדיא".

unique_minhagim.name: Koshchinon
unique_minhagim.description: The bride's first eyebrow shaping, done in the company of married women with songs and food.
unique_minhagim.description_he: עיצוב הגבות הראשון של הכלה, בחברת נשים נשואות עם שירים ומאכלים.

unique_minhagim.name: Tefillinbandon
unique_minhagim.description: Name of the bar mitzvah ceremony, literally 'tefillin-binding'.
unique_minhagim.description_he: שם טקס הבר מצווה, כלומר "קשירת תפילין" מילולית.

unique_minhagim.name: Sozanda
unique_minhagim.description: Women's ensembles of music and dance (three or four women) performing at weddings, circumcisions and other life-cycle celebrations in Bukhara and Samarkand.
unique_minhagim.description_he: הרכבי מוזיקה וריקוד של נשים (שלוש או ארבע) המופיעים בחתונות, בבריתות ובשמחות אחרות במחזור החיים בבוכרה ובסמרקנד.

disputes: Kitniyot on Pesach: three internal customs (no kitniyot at all; rice only; no rice on the first two days only). One community writer says the community eats kitniyot. R. Shalomayev says the restriction is not old and may come from Chabad influence.
Sheva brachot outside the couple's home: widespread current practice vs. Likutei Dinim, Mishmeret HaMinhagim and the Shulchan Aruch as read by R. Shalomayev.
Yushvo format: Torah-study evening (Likutei Dinim; R. Shalomayev) vs. the current large restaurant memorial dinner.
Blessing on samsa: mezonot (Ben Ish Chai, Kaf HaChaim, Taz) vs. hamotzi (R. Ovadia Yosef, Magen Avraham).

Pre-washing foods on Friday night: defended as a Sephardic practice vs. called a questionable unnecessary blessing (din.org.il).
